historical_record.description: A one-storey brick building with an ornate terra cotta cornice went up here in 1916 to the design of S. Heiman; it was demolished in 1979.

The San Francisco Mining Exchange Building was raised here in 1923 to the design of Miller & Pflueger, to house the exchange itself — unreinforced brick and masonry behind a decorative terra-cotta front, which the later tower was built around.
A one-storey brick building with an ornate terra cotta cornice went up here in 1923 to the design of T. Paterson Ross; it was demolished in 1979 and the lot left vacant.

The San Francisco Mining Exchange, founded in 1862 in the Montgomery Block and the second oldest exchange in the country, closed on 15 August 1967. The California State Chamber of Commerce and then the Western Title Insurance Company followed it into the building, which had stood empty since 1979.

The San Francisco Curb Exchange stood here. the Foundation for San Francisco's Architectural Heritage rated the San Francisco Curb Exchange "A" in the 1979 downtown survey it published as Splendid Survivors — the top of its four grades, which it reserved for the buildings it judged individually most important downtown. The Department of City Planning's 1976 Architectural Inventory coded it 3-D1-3.
The Mining Exchange Building on this corner was designated City Landmark No. 113 by Board of Supervisors ordinance 415-80, effective 5 October 1980.

unknowns: The 2025 assessor's roll dates this parcel 2018, long after the buildings described were demolished in 1979.

Two environmental reports name the building that stood on this corner differently: the 1981 initial study for 333 Bush Street calls it the San Francisco Curb Exchange, and the 1982 Russ Tower report calls it the San Francisco Mining Exchange Building.
